extracted.intended_audience: comedy writers, stand-up comedians, sketch writers, screenwriters, humorists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and evaluating running gags (recurring jokes/images) in comedy across verbal and visual media, focusing on repetition, variation, escalation, timing, and final payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance frequency (minimum occurrences)
rubrics_metrics.description: A running gag must repeat at least three times; fewer than three instances is considered a different device (Brick Joke or Chekhov's Gag).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count occurrences: three or more qualifies as a running gag. Anti-pattern: only one or two repeats — label/score as not a running gag. Examples: recurring car joke across a comedian's set; the Black Knight's repeated lines in Monty Python.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition as the source of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage repetition itself (Pavlovian conditioning) so humor accrues from repeated exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the gag so repetition increases comedic payoff over time. Scoring note: measure whether each occurrence yields additional laughter/recognition beyond the first. Example rationale: audience reward via pattern recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual incongruity (inappropriate context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the gag in contexts where it 'really shouldn't' occur to create additional humor through incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use surprise by inserting the recurring element into inappropriate or unexpected moments. Anti-pattern: always using the gag in similar, expected contexts makes it less funny. Example: a running gag that appears at solemn moments for contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bait-and-switch / substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up the expectation of the recurring gag but substitute something different to produce a twist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure occurrences so some return follow-throughs are replaced by alternative payoffs. This can refresh the gag and prevent predictability. Example: set up the usual punchline then deliver a variation or different outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modality: verbal versus visual running gags
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the running gag is verbal (recurring phrase, callback) or visual (recurring image/sight gag).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match mode to medium and performer strengths. Verbal examples: recurring catchphrases ('And don't call me Shirley'). Visual examples: a repeated sight gag or prop. Scoring: evaluate clarity and recognizability in chosen modality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing (when it returns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Control the timing of each recurrence — strategic placement affects recognition and impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan returns so they land at points that maximize surprise or anticipation. Consider pacing across the work (early, middle, late occurrences). Anti-pattern: returns that feel random or disrupt flow. Scoring: assess whether timing enhances comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition with variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each appearance should vary slightly rather than being identical every time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce small changes (phrasing, escalation, context) to keep the gag fresh and avoid staleness. Anti-pattern: exact repetition with no change reduces payoff. Example guidance from page: 'not identical each time.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup and audience anticipation / recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide sufficient setup so the audience recognizes the pattern and anticipates the gag before it lands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure early occurrences establish the pattern clearly; later occurrences can rely on audience anticipation. Scoring: does the audience anticipate the gag (pre-laughter) rather than being confused? Anti-pattern: insufficient setup leading to missed callbacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalation (raising stakes each time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each recurrence should escalate — increasing stakes, absurdity, or consequences to heighten humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design a series where each return raises the comedic payoff (bigger consequence, more extreme context). Scoring: evaluate whether escalation is perceptible and builds humor rather than plateauing. Example: progressively worsening outcomes for a recurring mishap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final twist / final subversion
rubrics_metrics.description: The last appearance often subverts the established pattern for a strong payoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan an endpoint that surprises by overturning expectations (final subversion). Scoring: assess whether the final twist provides closure and a heightened comedic payoff rather than undermining prior setup. Example rubric item: 'Is there a final subversion?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms of effectiveness (pattern recognition and community effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Underlying mechanisms that make running gags work: audience pattern recognition, inside-joke feeling, faster delivery on repeats, and anticipation creating pre-laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a running gag, consider whether it leverages these mechanisms: does it trigger recognition and a sense of shared knowledge? Are repeats faster and do they create pre-laughter? Use these signals as evidence of a successful running gag.
